pros: Optimal O(log n) time complexity for comparison-based search
Minimal space overhead: O(1) auxiliary memory
Simple and elegant algorithm, easy to understand
Information-theoretically optimal (achieves log n lower bound)
Iterative implementation avoids recursion stack overhead
Can be adapted for many variants (lower bound, upper bound, etc.)
Cache-efficient due to sequential memory access patterns
Works on any sorted random-access data structure (arrays, vectors)
Foundation for more complex data structures (B-trees, segment trees)
Can search over abstract monotonic functions, not just arrays
cons: Requires sorted input (sorting adds O(n log n) preprocessing cost)
Only works with random-access data structures (not linked lists)
Inefficient for small n (linear search may be faster due to branch prediction)
Recursive implementation uses O(log n) stack space
Integer overflow vulnerability in naive midpoint calculation
Multiple variants needed for duplicate elements (lower/upper bound)
Cannot handle dynamic datasets with frequent insertions/deletions
Poor cache performance for very large arrays that don't fit in cache
Requires comparison operator to be well-defined and transitive
Not suitable for external memory (disk-based) search directly
Performance degrades if array is not randomly accessible
